questions.q: A worker's wage rises and she chooses to work fewer hours. Which statement best explains this?
options: The substitution effect outweighs the income effect
The income effect outweighs the substitution effect
Leisure must be an inferior good
questions.why: The substitution effect always pushes hours up when the wage rises. Fewer hours means the income effect, which with leisure a normal good reduces hours, dominated.

questions.q: A monopsonist faces labour supply w = 2 + 0.25L and marginal revenue product MRP = 20 − 0.5L. How many workers does it hire and at what wage?
questions.why: Total wage cost is 2L + 0.25L², so MCL = 2 + 0.5L. Setting this equal to 20 − 0.5L gives L = 18, and the supply curve gives w = 2 + 4.5 = 6.5. L = 24, w = 8 is the competitive outcome.

questions.q: Why are OLS estimates of the return to schooling thought to be biased upward?
options: Unobserved ability is positively correlated with both schooling and earnings
Experience is included as a control
questions.why: Omitted ability raises both schooling and wages, which inflates the schooling coefficient. Measurement error works the other way, biasing it towards zero.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of a pure public good?
questions.why: Flood defence protecting an area is non-rival and non-excludable. A toll road and a pool are excludable (club goods), and a fishery is rival (a common-pool resource).

questions.q: Demand is P = 120 − 2Q and supply is P = 20 + 3Q. A specific tax of £10 per unit is levied on sellers. How much of the tax per unit is borne by consumers?
questions.why: Equilibrium moves from Q = 20, P = 80 to Q = 18 with buyers paying 84 and sellers receiving 74. Consumers bear £4 and producers £6, because demand is the more elastic side here.

questions.q: Compulsory social insurance is most directly justified as a solution to which problem?
questions.why: Compulsion keeps low-risk people in the pool, preventing the adverse-selection death spiral. It does nothing to reduce moral hazard, which compulsion can if anything worsen.

questions.q: In the Foster-Greer-Thorbecke family, which measure changes when income is transferred from a poor person to a poorer person, with both staying below the line?
questions.why: P₀ counts the poor and P₁ sums their gaps, so neither changes. P₂ weights larger gaps more heavily, so it falls when the poorest gain.

questions.q: Country A can produce 1 car or 4 tonnes of wheat with a unit of labour. Country B can produce 1 car or 2 tonnes of wheat. Which statement is correct?
options: A has a comparative advantage in both goods
A has a comparative advantage in wheat and B in cars
B has a comparative advantage in wheat
No gains from trade exist because both are equally good at cars
questions.why: A car costs 4 tonnes of wheat in A but only 2 in B, so B has the comparative advantage in cars. A's opportunity cost of wheat (¼ car) is below B's (½ car), so A has the comparative advantage in wheat.

questions.q: In the Heckscher-Ohlin model, a capital-abundant country opens to trade. According to Stolper-Samuelson, what happens?
options: Real wages and real returns to capital both rise
The real return to capital rises and the real wage falls
The real wage rises and the real return to capital falls
questions.why: The relative price of the capital-intensive export good rises. This raises the real return to capital and lowers the real wage, so there are winners and losers even though aggregate welfare rises.

questions.q: A customs union causes a member to switch its imports of a good from a low-cost non-member to a higher-cost partner. This is:
questions.why: Viner's (1950) trade diversion replaces cheaper outside supply with costlier partner supply, which can reduce welfare.

questions.q: According to Weitzman (1974), when abatement costs are uncertain, a carbon tax is preferable to a cap if:
options: the marginal damage curve is steeper than the marginal abatement cost curve
the marginal damage curve is flatter than the marginal abatement cost curve
abatement costs are known with certainty
questions.why: A flat marginal damage curve means errors in quantity are cheap but errors in price are costly, so fixing the price is better. CO₂, a stock pollutant, has fairly flat short-run marginal damage.

questions.q: Using the labour-leisure model, explain why an in-work benefit paid only to those who work at least 16 hours a week may raise employment but reduce hours among some existing workers.
markScheme: Benefit raises the return to working ≥16 hours relative to not working
For non-workers the participation incentive rises (extensive margin up)
Workers already above 16 hours get an income effect, reducing hours if leisure is normal
Some may cut hours towards the 16-hour threshold, causing bunching; the net effect on total hours is ambiguous
questions.modelAnswer: The benefit creates a jump in the budget constraint at 16 hours. For someone not working, the payoff from taking a job of at least 16 hours rises, so more people participate: the extensive margin. For someone already working, say, 35 hours, the benefit is extra income that does not change the marginal wage. With leisure a normal good, the income effect leads them to cut hours. Some will move to exactly 16 hours to keep the benefit with less work, producing bunching at the threshold. Employment rises, but the effect on total hours is ambiguous.

questions.q: Explain how Spence's signalling model differs from human capital theory and why the distinction matters for education policy.
markScheme: Human capital: education raises productivity, so higher wages reflect higher output
Signalling: education costs less for high-ability people, so it separates types without raising productivity
Both predict a positive wage-education correlation, so OLS cannot distinguish them
Policy: under signalling, the social return is below the private return, so subsidies may be wasteful; under human capital, subsidies may correct underinvestment
questions.modelAnswer: Human capital theory says education makes workers more productive, so employers pay more for educated workers because they produce more. In Spence's (1973) signalling model, education may teach nothing useful. It is simply less costly for high-ability people to complete, so obtaining a degree reveals ability to employers who cannot observe it directly. Both models predict that educated people earn more, so a simple earnings regression cannot separate them. The policy stakes are large. If education is mainly a signal, the social return is below the private return and expanding it leads to credential inflation. If it builds skills, subsidies can correct underinvestment caused by credit constraints.

questions.q: A market has demand P = 120 − 2Q and supply P = 20 + 3Q, and a specific tax of £10 per unit is levied on sellers. Calculate the tax revenue and deadweight loss, and verify the consumers' share of the burden using elasticities at the original equilibrium.
markScheme: With tax: Q = 18, P_d = 84, P_s = 74
Consumer share = ε_S/(ε_S + |ε_D|) = (4/3)/(10/3) = 0.4, matching £4 of £10
questions.modelAnswer: With the tax, 120 − 2Q = 20 + 3Q + 10, so Q = 18. Buyers pay 120 − 36 = £84 and sellers keep £74. Revenue is 10 × 18 = £180. The deadweight loss is the triangle of trades lost: ½ × 10 × (20 − 18) = £10. At the original equilibrium (Q = 20, P = 80), the demand elasticity is (1/2)(80/20) = 2 and the supply elasticity is (1/3)(80/20) = 4/3. The consumers' share is ε_S/(ε_S + |ε_D|) = 0.4, so consumers bear £4 and producers £6, matching the price changes.

questions.q: Ellie, a lone parent on Universal Credit, earns above her work allowance. She pays 20% income tax and 8% employee National Insurance on extra earnings, and UC is withdrawn at 55% of net earnings. Calculate her effective marginal tax rate and explain one consequence.
markScheme: From £1 extra gross: tax and NI = 28p, net = 72p
UC withdrawn = 0.55 × 72p = 39.6p
Consequence: weakens incentives to increase hours or seek promotion (intensive margin); trade-off with cost of lower taper
questions.modelAnswer: From an extra £1 of gross pay, income tax and NI take 28p, leaving 72p net. Universal Credit is withdrawn at 55% of net earnings: 0.55 × 72p = 39.6p. She loses 28 + 39.6 = 67.6p in total, an EMTR of 67.6%, keeping only 32.4p. This is far higher than the 28% faced by a basic-rate taxpayer not on benefits, and it weakens her incentive to increase hours or take a better-paid job. Lowering the taper would help but would extend entitlement further up the income scale and cost more.

questions.q: Six people have daily incomes of 2, 3, 5, 8, 12 and 20, and the poverty line is 6. Calculate the headcount ratio, the poverty gap index and the minimum total transfer needed to eliminate poverty with perfect targeting.
markScheme: Poor: 2, 3, 5, so headcount = 3/6 = 0.5
Normalised gaps: 4/6, 3/6, 1/6
Minimum transfer = sum of absolute gaps = 4 + 3 + 1 = 8
questions.modelAnswer: Three of the six people are below 6, so the headcount ratio is 0.5. Their shortfalls are 4, 3 and 1, or 4/6, 3/6 and 1/6 of the line. The poverty gap index averages these over the whole population: (8/6)/6 ≈ 0.222. Lifting everyone exactly to the line requires transfers equal to the total shortfall, 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 a day. That is the poverty gap expressed in money (P₁ × N × z = 0.222 × 6 × 6 = 8). In practice targeting is imperfect and costs more.

questions.q: Explain how Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001) used settler mortality to identify the effect of institutions on income, and one criticism of the approach.
markScheme: Problem: institutions and income are jointly determined (reverse causality, omitted variables)
Instrument: settler mortality shaped colonisation strategy (settlement versus extraction), which shaped early and hence current institutions
Exclusion restriction: mortality affects income today only through institutions
Criticism: Albouy (2012) on data quality, or mortality may affect income via disease environment/geography/human capital (exclusion violated)
questions.modelAnswer: Rich countries can afford good institutions, so a simple regression of income on institutions confuses cause and effect. AJR argued that where European settlers faced high mortality, colonisers set up extractive institutions; where settlers could survive, they built institutions protecting property. Those institutions persisted. Settler mortality is used as an instrument that shifts institutions but is assumed to affect income today only through them. The 2SLS estimates show a large effect of institutions. Critics such as Albouy (2012) questioned the reliability of the mortality data. Others argue that mortality reflects disease environments that affect income directly, which would violate the exclusion restriction.

questions.q: Explain why trade between similar countries, such as cars traded between France and Germany, is hard to explain with Heckscher-Ohlin and how Krugman's model explains it.
markScheme: H-O relies on differences in factor endowments; similar countries have little reason to trade
Krugman: increasing returns mean each firm produces a differentiated variety at scale
Consumers love variety, so countries both export and import varieties of the same good (intra-industry trade), gaining from variety and lower average costs
questions.modelAnswer: Heckscher-Ohlin explains trade through differences in relative factor endowments. France and Germany have similar endowments and still trade large volumes of cars in both directions. Krugman (1979, 1980) combines increasing returns to scale with consumers' love of variety. Each firm specialises in a differentiated variety, produced at scale to lower average costs, and sells it in both markets. Trade lets consumers in each country access more varieties at lower prices: intra-industry trade with gains even between identical countries.

questions.q: A car sells for £10,000 on the world market and uses imported components worth £6,000 at world prices. A country imposes a 20% tariff on cars and a 5% tariff on components. Calculate the effective rate of protection for domestic car assembly and interpret it.
markScheme: Value added at world prices = 10,000 − 6,000 = 4,000
Domestic car price 12,000; component cost 6,300; domestic value added = 5,700
Interpretation: protection of assembly is more than double the nominal 20% tariff because inputs are taxed at a lower rate
questions.modelAnswer: At world prices assemblers add 10,000 − 6,000 = £4,000 of value. With tariffs, the car sells for £12,000 domestically and the components cost £6,300, so domestic value added is £5,700. The effective rate of protection is (5,700 − 4,000)/4,000 = 42.5%. Although the nominal tariff on cars is 20%, the assembly activity enjoys protection of over 40%, because its output is protected more heavily than its inputs. Tariff escalation like this can draw resources into activities that are not competitive at world prices.

questions.q: Explain why the choice of discount rate is so important for the social cost of carbon. Illustrate with a damage of £1,000 occurring in 100 years, discounted at 1.4% and 4.1%.
markScheme: Climate damages occur far in the future, so PV is very sensitive to r
Ramsey rule r = ρ + ηg: Stern-type parameters (ρ = 0.1%, η = 1, g = 1.3%) give 1.4%; higher ρ and η give rates like 4.1%; this is an ethical as well as empirical choice
questions.modelAnswer: The damages from a tonne of CO₂ emitted today are spread over centuries, so compounding makes their present value very sensitive to the discount rate. £1,000 of damage in 100 years is worth 1,000/1.014¹⁰⁰ ≈ £249 today at 1.4%, but only 1,000/1.041¹⁰⁰ ≈ £18 at 4.1%, a fourteen-fold difference. Under the Ramsey rule r = ρ + ηg, Stern-style parameters (ρ = 0.1%, η = 1, g = 1.3%) give 1.4%. A higher time preference and greater inequality aversion (ρ = 1.5%, η = 2) give 4.1%. Choosing ρ is largely an ethical judgement about future generations.

questions.q: Why is the economically efficient level of pollution usually greater than zero?
markScheme: Abatement has rising marginal costs while the marginal damage of the last units is low
Efficiency requires MAC = MD, which occurs at a positive level of emissions
questions.modelAnswer: Cutting pollution is costly, and each extra unit of abatement typically costs more than the last. The damage from the final few units of pollution is often small. Eliminating them entirely would cost more than the harm avoided. Efficiency is reached where the marginal cost of abating one more unit equals the marginal damage it causes, and that usually occurs at a positive level of emissions.

questions.q:
Moorside is a remote town where Calloway Foods is the only significant employer. Labour supply to the firm is w = 2 + 0.25L and the marginal revenue product of labour is MRP = 20 − 0.5L, where L is workers (hundreds) and w is the hourly wage (£).
(a) Find the employment and wage under perfect competition and under monopsony.
(b) Calculate the deadweight loss of monopsony.
(c) The government imposes a minimum wage of £10. Find the new employment level.
(d) Over what range of minimum wages does employment exceed the monopsony level?
(e) Discuss what the empirical literature suggests about minimum wages in practice.
markScheme: Competitive: 2 + 0.25L = 20 − 0.5L, so L = 24, w = 8
Monopsony: MCL = 2 + 0.5L; set equal to MRP gives L = 18, w = 6.5
At w_min = 10: supply would be 32 but demand (MRP = 10) is L = 20; employment = 20
Range: above 6.5 and below MRP at L = 18, which is 11 (employment > 18 for 6.5 < w_min < 11)
Maximum employment at w_min = 8 (competitive level)
Card and Krueger (1994); Neumark and Wascher critique
Cengiz et al. (2019) bunching; UK Low Pay Commission evidence of small effects
Caveats: effects may appear in hours, prices or automation; large rises relative to median may cause losses
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Under competition, supply equals MRP: 2 + 0.25L = 20 − 0.5L, so L = 24 and w = £8. A monopsonist must raise the wage for all workers to hire one more, so total wage cost is 2L + 0.25L² and MCL = 2 + 0.5L. Setting MCL = MRP gives 2 + 0.5L = 20 − 0.5L, so L = 18. It pays the lowest wage that attracts 18: w = 2 + 4.5 = £6.50.

(b) Between L = 18 and 24, workers' marginal product exceeds their reservation wage but they are not hired. DWL = ½ × (MRP(18) − w(18)) × 6 = ½ × (11 − 6.5) × 6 = 13.5 (£ × hundreds of workers per hour).

(c) With a £10 floor, the firm's marginal cost of labour is flat at £10 until the supply curve, which reaches 10 at L = 32. The firm hires where MRP = 10: 20 − 0.5L = 10, so L = 20. Employment rises from 18 to 20 and the wage from £6.50 to £10.

(d) Employment exceeds 18 for any minimum wage above £6.50 and below MRP(18) = £11. It peaks at 24 when the minimum equals the competitive wage of £8. Above £11 employment falls below the monopsony level.

(e) Card and Krueger (1994) found no fall in New Jersey fast-food employment after a minimum wage rise, consistent with monopsony. Neumark and Wascher challenged their data. More recent work by Cengiz et al. (2019) finds that moderate increases destroy few jobs. UK evidence from the Low Pay Commission on the National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage points the same way, even as the NLW reached two-thirds of median earnings. Caveats remain. Adjustment may come through hours, prices, profits or long-run automation, and very high minimums relative to local median wages, especially in poorer regions, could breach the monopsony range and cut jobs. Calloway's isolated position makes the monopsony model particularly plausible here.

questions.q:
Tom has 100 hours a week available, utility U = ln C + ln L (L is leisure) and non-labour income V. He earns wage w per hour.
(a) Derive his labour supply function h(w, V).
(b) Calculate his hours when w = £10 and V = £200, and when w = £15 and V = £200.
(c) Calculate his hours when w = £10 and V = 0, and explain why the wage rise in (b) increases hours when V = £200 but would not if V = 0.
(d) The government introduces a lump-sum benefit of £200 a week, withdrawn at 50p per £1 earned until exhausted. Explain qualitatively how this affects his labour supply and the policy dilemma it illustrates.
markScheme: Budget: C = w(100 − L) + V, so full income = 100w + V
Cobb-Douglas: spend half on leisure, so wL = (100w + V)/2
V = 0: h = 50 regardless of w (income and substitution effects cancel)
With V > 0, a wage rise raises hours because the income effect is proportionately smaller (V is not scaled by w)
Taper lowers the effective net wage to 0.5w while benefit exhausts, giving a substitution effect that reduces hours
Benefit raises income, so an income effect also lowers hours
Dilemma: targeting (high taper) versus work incentives (low taper, higher cost)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Full income is 100w + V, spent on consumption and leisure (priced at w). With U = ln C + ln L, Tom spends half of full income on each, so wL = (100w + V)/2 and L = 50 + V/(2w). Hours are h = 100 − L = 50 − V/(2w).

(b) At w = 10 and V = 200: h = 50 − 200/20 = 40 hours. At w = 15: h = 50 − 200/30 ≈ 43.3 hours. The wage rise increases hours.

(c) With V = 0, h = 50 whatever the wage. With Cobb-Douglas preferences and no unearned income, the substitution effect of a higher wage is exactly offset by the income effect, so hours do not respond. When V > 0, part of his income does not scale with the wage, so a wage rise raises full income less than proportionately. The income effect is weaker relative to the substitution effect, and hours rise.

(d) The benefit gives £200 when he does not work, withdrawn at 50% of earnings. While the benefit is still being withdrawn, each hour worked raises net income by only 0.5w, which halves the effective wage. The substitution effect then lowers hours. The benefit also raises income at low hours, an income effect that further reduces hours. Some people who would have worked a little may stop entirely. With w = 10, the benefit is exhausted after £400 of earnings, or 40 hours. At Tom's original 40 hours he would gain nothing, so he will probably cut hours sharply. This illustrates the classic trade-off. A steep taper targets support on the poorest cheaply but creates high effective marginal tax rates. A gentle taper protects incentives but extends payments up the income scale and costs more. That is the logic behind the UK cutting the Universal Credit taper to 55% and the case for in-work credits.

questions.q: "The rise in earnings inequality in the UK and US since 1980 is best explained by technological change." Discuss.
markScheme: Describes the facts: rising 90/10 and top shares; UK sharp rise in 1980s then flatter Gini; graduate premium
Skill-biased technical change and race between education and technology (Goldin and Katz 2008)
Supply side: graduate expansion slowed relative premium growth
Task-based model and polarisation (Autor, Levy and Murnane 2003; Goos and Manning 2007): SBTC alone cannot explain middle hollowing
Trade and offshoring: China shock (Autor, Dorn and Hanson 2013), Stolper-Samuelson
Institutions: union decline, minimum wages (DiNardo, Fortin and Lemieux 1996 for US); UK NMW compressing bottom from 1999
Top incomes: Piketty and Saez on top pay, taxes and bargaining; superstar firms
Taxes and transfers: market versus disposable income inequality
Evaluation of relative importance and timing; cross-country differences with similar technology suggest institutions matter
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Earnings inequality rose sharply in both countries from around 1980. In the UK the Gini coefficient jumped in the 1980s and has been broadly flat since the early 1990s. In the US the 90/10 ratio and top income shares kept rising. Any explanation must fit these timings.

The technology account is powerful. Skill-biased technical change, especially computerisation, raised the relative demand for graduates. Goldin and Katz (2008) frame wage inequality as a race between education and technology: when the supply of graduates lags demand, the premium rises. The US slowdown in college expansion after 1980 fits this well. Task-based models refine the story. Autor, Levy and Murnane (2003) show that computers substitute for routine cognitive and manual tasks while complementing abstract work. This explains job polarisation, the growth of both high- and low-wage jobs at the expense of the middle, documented for the UK by Goos and Manning (2007). Simple SBTC cannot explain polarisation on its own.

Other forces matter. Trade with low-wage economies, through Stolper-Samuelson logic and the China shock (Autor, Dorn and Hanson, 2013), hurt manufacturing workers in exposed regions, though most estimates attribute a smaller share of aggregate inequality to trade than to technology. Institutions are critical. Union density fell steeply in the UK after 1979 and the real US minimum wage eroded. DiNardo, Fortin and Lemieux (1996) attribute a large share of rising US wage dispersion to these changes. Conversely, the UK's National Minimum Wage compressed the bottom of the distribution after 1999. At the very top, Piketty and Saez link soaring executive pay to lower top tax rates and bargaining power rather than marginal productivity, and superstar-firm dynamics also play a role.

Cross-country evidence is telling. Continental European countries adopted similar technologies but saw much smaller rises in inequality, which suggests that institutions and education systems mediate technology's effects.

Technology is therefore the most important common driver, especially of the graduate premium and polarisation. But "best explained" overstates it. Institutions and policy explain much of the cross-country variation, the UK's distinctive 1980s spike and the top-end surge.

questions.q:
Ashgrove Chemicals discharges effluent into a river used by Riverbend Fisheries. Ashgrove's marginal private benefit from production is MPB = 100 − Q, and its marginal private cost is constant at 20. Each unit of output causes marginal external damage to Riverbend of MED = 0.5Q.
(a) Find the private (unregulated) and socially efficient output levels.
(b) Calculate the deadweight loss from the externality.
(c) What Pigouvian tax would achieve efficiency?
(d) Explain how the Coase theorem suggests the parties might reach efficiency without government, and why this may fail.
(e) Compare a Pigouvian tax with a fixed output quota.
markScheme: Private: 100 − Q = 20, so Q = 80
DWL = area between MSC and MPB from 53.3 to 80 = ½ × (80 − 53.3) × (MSC(80) − MPB(80)) = ½ × 26.7 × 40 ≈ 533
Pigouvian tax = MED at the optimum = 0.5 × 53.3 ≈ £26.67 per unit
Coase: assign rights; if Riverbend has rights, Ashgrove pays to pollute; if Ashgrove has rights, Riverbend pays to reduce output; either way Q ≈ 53.3
Distribution differs with rights, efficiency does not
Failure: transaction costs, many parties, information asymmetry, holdout, wealth effects
Tax versus quota: tax raises revenue and is dynamically efficient; quota needs information; with one firm both can reach the optimum if set correctly; tax adapts if costs change
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Unregulated, Ashgrove sets MPB = MPC: 100 − Q = 20, so Q = 80. Socially, marginal social cost is 20 + 0.5Q, so 100 − Q = 20 + 0.5Q gives 1.5Q = 80 and Q ≈ 53.3.

(b) For units between 53.3 and 80, social cost exceeds benefit. At Q = 80, MSC = 60 and MPB = 20, a gap of 40. At Q = 53.3 the gap is zero. DWL = ½ × (80 − 53.3) × 40 ≈ 533.

(c) A Pigouvian tax equal to marginal external damage at the optimum is 0.5 × 53.3 ≈ £26.67 per unit. Ashgrove then faces cost 46.67 and sets 100 − Q = 46.67, so Q = 53.3.

(d) Coase (1960) argued that if property rights over the river are clear and bargaining is cheap, the parties will reach Q ≈ 53.3 whoever holds the rights. If Riverbend has the right to a clean river, Ashgrove will pay it to accept pollution for units where Ashgrove's net benefit exceeds the damage. If Ashgrove has the right to pollute, Riverbend will pay it to cut output beyond 53.3, since its damage exceeds Ashgrove's lost profit there. Only the distribution of gains differs. Bargaining may fail, however, if there are many affected parties (anglers, households), if damages are hard to verify, if either side has private information and bluffs, or if legal and negotiation costs are high. Wealth effects can also matter.

(e) With a single firm and full information, a quota of 53.3 achieves the same output as the tax. The tax raises revenue that can reduce other distorting taxes, gives a continuing incentive to find cleaner methods, and adjusts automatically if Ashgrove's benefits change. A quota requires the regulator to know the optimal quantity and gives no reason to go beyond it. With uncertain costs, Weitzman's analysis guides the choice. A better-targeted instrument would tax the effluent itself rather than output, encouraging abatement technology rather than just lower production.

questions.q: "The top rate of income tax should be set to maximise the revenue raised from top earners." Critically evaluate this proposition with reference to optimal tax theory and evidence.
markScheme: Mirrlees (1971) framework: equity-efficiency trade-off
Diamond and Saez (2011) top rate τ = 1/(1 + a × e) derived as revenue-maximising when social welfare weight on top earners → 0
Example: a = 1.5, e = 0.25 gives ≈ 73%; e = 0.5 gives ≈ 57%
Elasticity of taxable income includes hours, effort, avoidance, timing, migration
Evidence: UK 50% rate 2010 and forestalling/income shifting (HMRC 2012); Kleven et al. on migration of footballers
Piketty, Saez and Stantcheva (2014): bargaining component means e from avoidance or bargaining should be treated differently; real supply elasticity may be low
Avoidance elasticity depends on tax base design, so policy can lower e
Objections: positive welfare weight on top earners, or libertarian/desert arguments, imply lower rate
Fiscal externalities (corporate tax shifting) and spillovers (innovation, entrepreneurship)
Laffer curve logic; revenue maximum is upper bound
Conclusion: Rawlsian/utilitarian with concave utility supports near revenue-maximising rate, but uncertainty and base-broadening matter
questions.modelAnswer:
Optimal tax theory, following Mirrlees (1971), trades off redistribution against the efficiency costs of discouraging work and income generation. For the very top, Diamond and Saez (2011) show that if society places negligible marginal welfare weight on extra income for top earners, the optimal top rate is the one that maximises revenue from them: τ = 1/(1 + a × e). Here a is the Pareto parameter describing how thick the top tail is, and e is the elasticity of taxable income. With a ≈ 1.5 and e = 0.25 this gives about 73% (including all taxes on earnings); with e = 0.5 it falls to about 57%.

Its practical force depends on e, which captures not only hours and effort but also avoidance, income shifting, timing and migration. UK evidence is instructive. When the 50% additional rate was introduced in 2010, many high earners brought forward income before its start, and HMRC's 2012 assessment suggested a high taxable-income elasticity and little net revenue. That estimate was uncertain because forestalling distorted the short window. Kleven, Landais and Saez (2013) found that top footballers' location responds to tax rates.

Piketty, Saez and Stantcheva (2014) refine the analysis. If part of the response is executives bargaining for higher pay at others' expense, that response is not a real efficiency cost, and the optimal rate rises. If the response is avoidance, it depends on policy: broadening the base and closing shifting channels lowers e and raises the revenue-maximising rate. Conversely, positive spillovers from entrepreneurship and innovation would argue for a lower rate.

The ethical premise can also be challenged. Utilitarian weights are small but not zero, which implies a rate somewhat below the revenue maximum. Desert-based or libertarian views reject the premise that top incomes are simply a resource to be maximised. Higher personal rates may also shift income into corporate or capital forms.

The revenue-maximising rate is best seen as an upper bound and a useful benchmark rather than a target. Its location depends on base design and elasticities, so base-broadening should come first.

questions.q: "Unemployment benefits mainly discourage people from finding work. Governments should cut them." Evaluate this claim using economic theory and evidence.
markScheme: Rationale for public UI: private market failure via adverse selection and correlated risk
Consumption smoothing benefit: concave utility, borrowing constraints
Moral hazard: lower search effort, higher reservation wage, longer spells
Baily (1978)/Chetty (2006) optimal UI formula balances these
Chetty (2008): liquidity versus moral hazard; liquidity effect is welfare-improving
Evidence: duration elasticities; spike in exits when benefits expire
Match quality: longer search may improve job matches
Macroeconomic stabiliser in recessions; optimal UI may be countercyclical
Design alternatives: conditionality, job search requirements, declining benefit profiles, UI savings accounts
UK context: low replacement rate of Jobseeker's Allowance/Universal Credit relative to OECD
Balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Private unemployment insurance markets barely exist. People at high risk of unemployment are the most likely to buy cover (adverse selection), and job losses are correlated in recessions, which makes risk hard to diversify. Public UI fills this gap. Its central benefit is consumption smoothing: with diminishing marginal utility and limited savings, a sharp fall in consumption on job loss is very costly in welfare terms.

The claim stresses the cost side. By making unemployment less painful, benefits raise reservation wages and reduce search effort, which lengthens spells. Durations do rise with generosity, and exits to work often spike when benefits expire.

Baily (1978) and Chetty (2006) show that optimal benefits balance the marginal consumption-smoothing gain against the marginal moral-hazard cost. The fact that UI lengthens spells does not by itself show that benefits are too high. Chetty (2008) went further. Using US data, he found that a large share of the duration response comes from a liquidity effect. Cash-constrained workers rush into the first available job, and benefits let them search properly. That response is welfare-improving, not a distortion. Longer search can also produce better matches with higher wages and tenure, although evidence on match quality is mixed.

There is also a macroeconomic argument. UI acts as an automatic stabiliser, sustaining demand in downturns. When jobs are scarce, the moral-hazard cost of extra benefits is smaller because extra search effort finds fewer jobs. This supports more generous UI in recessions, as with US benefit extensions after 2008 and in 2020.

Design matters as much as the level. Job-search requirements, conditionality and active labour-market programmes can limit moral hazard. Declining benefit profiles target support early in a spell. UI savings accounts are another option. The UK already has one of the lowest unemployment benefit replacement rates in the OECD, with Universal Credit standard allowances paid at a flat rate, so the case for further cuts there is weak.

The claim captures a real disincentive but misreads its welfare implications. The evidence supports well-designed, conditional benefits, with generosity varying over the cycle, rather than blanket cuts.

questions.q: "Population ageing makes pay-as-you-go state pensions unsustainable, so countries should shift to fully funded systems." Discuss.
markScheme: Explains PAYG: current workers fund current pensioners; implicit return = n + g (Samuelson 1958, Aaron 1966)
Funded: contributions invested; return r
Ageing raises dependency ratio, so PAYG requires higher contributions, lower benefits or later retirement
Aaron condition: funded better in steady state if r > n + g
Transition problem: one generation pays twice; switching is not a free lunch, since the PAYG implicit debt is real (Barr 2002)
Funded systems are also exposed to ageing: asset meltdown, lower returns if savings glut; Barr's point that output is what matters
Risks: investment, annuity and inflation risk transferred to individuals; administrative costs (Chile experience)
PAYG offers intergenerational risk-sharing and redistribution
Adjustment levers: State Pension age increases (UK to 67 from 2026–28), indexation (triple lock cost), auto-enrolment as funded pillar
Conclusion: multi-pillar mix; sustainability is about parameters not funding method alone
questions.modelAnswer:
Under a pay-as-you-go system, today's workers' contributions pay today's pensioners. Samuelson (1958) and Aaron (1966) showed that its implicit return equals the growth rate of the wage bill: population growth n plus productivity growth g. A funded system invests contributions in assets, earning the market return r. Ageing, with fewer workers per pensioner, lowers n and raises the dependency ratio. A PAYG scheme must then raise contributions, cut benefits or raise the pension age.

The case for funding rests on the Aaron condition. If r > n + g, as is often the case, a funded system offers higher returns in steady state.

The move is far from a free lunch. Existing PAYG promises are an implicit public debt. During a transition, one generation must both fund its own pensions and continue paying current pensioners: the "double burden". Financing the transition with explicit debt merely converts implicit debt into explicit debt, with no net gain unless saving rises. Barr (2002) stresses a more fundamental point. Pensioners' consumption must come from the output of current workers whatever the financing method. Funded systems are also exposed to ageing, because when large cohorts retire and sell assets, asset prices and returns may fall.

Funded defined-contribution systems shift investment, inflation and longevity risk onto individuals and can carry high administrative charges. Chile's 1981 privatisation became the standard illustration of low coverage and costly fees, and it was later reformed with a solidarity pillar. PAYG systems, by contrast, allow risk-sharing across generations and redistribution to low earners.

Ageing can be managed within PAYG through its parameters. The UK has legislated State Pension age rises (to 67 between 2026 and 2028, with 68 scheduled later), while the triple lock raises long-run costs. The UK has also built a funded pillar through automatic enrolment since 2012, which raised workplace pension participation sharply, consistent with Madrian and Shea's (2001) default effects.

Ageing does strain PAYG, but sustainability depends on contribution rates, retirement ages and indexation, not on funding alone. Most economists favour a multi-pillar mix: a PAYG base for poverty relief and risk-sharing, alongside funded saving.

questions.q: "Randomised controlled trials have transformed development economics, but they cannot tell us how countries escape poverty." Discuss.
markScheme: Explains RCTs: random assignment solves selection bias, giving credible causal estimates
Contributions: deworming (Miguel and Kremer 2004), CCTs (PROGRESA), GiveDirectly cash transfers, microcredit (Banerjee, Karlan and Zinman 2015)
Nobel 2019 (Banerjee, Duflo, Kremer); policy influence and evidence-based aid
External validity (Deaton 2010; Deaton and Cartwright 2018): context dependence, scaling issues, general-equilibrium effects
Narrow questions: micro interventions versus macro drivers
Macro evidence on growth: Solow convergence, institutions (Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson 2001), structural transformation (Lewis), East Asian industrial policy
Big development transitions (China, South Korea) owed to macro and institutional change, not RCT-tested programmes
Counter: RCTs can test macro-relevant mechanisms (e.g. Egger et al. 2022 GE effects of cash transfers in Kenya), and improve state capacity
Ethical concerns
Balanced conclusion: complementary tools
questions.modelAnswer:
RCTs randomly assign an intervention, so treated and control groups differ only by chance and the difference in outcomes identifies the causal effect. This solves the selection bias that plagued earlier evaluations. The movement, recognised by the 2019 Nobel prize for Banerjee, Duflo and Kremer, has produced influential findings. Mexico's PROGRESA raised school enrolment (Schultz, 2004). Unconditional cash transfers through GiveDirectly raised consumption and assets (Haushofer and Shapiro, 2016). Six microcredit RCTs found only modest average gains (Banerjee, Karlan and Zinman, 2015), deflating earlier hype. Deworming was shown to raise school attendance (Miguel and Kremer, 2004), although re-analyses dispute the magnitude. These results reshaped aid spending and government programmes.

The critique has force. Deaton (2010) argues that RCTs estimate average effects in specific contexts and say little about why programmes work, which limits external validity. Effects can change at scale, when governments rather than NGOs implement, or when general-equilibrium effects such as price changes kick in. RCTs also favour questions that can be randomised, such as textbooks, bed nets or reminders, while the forces behind the great escapes from poverty are largely macroeconomic and institutional. South Korea, Taiwan and China grew rich through capital accumulation, structural transformation from agriculture to manufacturing in the Lewis tradition, export orientation and state capacity. Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001) link long-run prosperity to institutions. None of these can be randomised.

The division is not absolute. Some RCTs now test general-equilibrium effects directly. Egger et al. (2022) randomised cash transfers across Kenyan villages and found large local multiplier effects with little inflation. Experiments also inform state capacity, for example on tax collection and civil service incentives, which matters for growth. Macro questions are studied with natural experiments and quasi-experimental methods inspired by the same credibility revolution.

RCTs have transformed how development economists establish causality at the micro level and have improved the allocation of aid. They are not a theory of growth. Escaping mass poverty depends on institutions, investment and structural change, which require historical, macro and political-economy evidence alongside experimental findings.

questions.q:
Home and Foreign each produce cloth and wheat using only labour. In Home, a unit of cloth takes 1 hour and a unit of wheat 2 hours. In Foreign, cloth takes 6 hours and wheat 4 hours. Home has 120 hours of labour and Foreign 240.
(a) Identify absolute and comparative advantage.
(b) Within what range must the world terms of trade lie for both to gain?
(c) Suppose the terms of trade settle at 1 cloth per unit of wheat with complete specialisation. Show the gains for each country.
(d) Discuss two limitations of the Ricardian model as an explanation of real-world trade.
markScheme: Home has absolute advantage in both goods (fewer hours each)
Opportunity cost of wheat: Home 2 cloth; Foreign 4/6 ≈ 0.67 cloth
Home comparative advantage in cloth; Foreign in wheat
Terms of trade between 0.67 and 2 cloth per wheat
Home specialises: 120 cloth; Foreign: 60 wheat
Home gains: each wheat now costs 1 cloth instead of 2 (one hour versus two)
Foreign gains: each cloth costs 1 wheat (4 hours) instead of 1.5 wheat (6 hours)
Real wage rises in terms of the imported good in both countries
Limitations: one factor so no distributional effects (contrast H-O/Stolper-Samuelson, specific factors)
Limitations: complete specialisation is unrealistic; ignores increasing returns, intra-industry trade, trade costs
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Home needs fewer hours for both goods (1 versus 6 for cloth, 2 versus 4 for wheat), so it has an absolute advantage in both. Comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost. In Home a unit of wheat costs 2 cloth; in Foreign it costs 4/6 ≈ 0.67 cloth. Foreign has the comparative advantage in wheat, and Home in cloth, where its opportunity cost is 0.5 wheat against Foreign's 1.5.

(b) Both gain if the price of wheat lies between the autarky opportunity costs: between 0.67 and 2 cloth per unit of wheat. Home then buys wheat for less than 2 cloth, and Foreign sells wheat for more than 0.67 cloth.

(c) Home specialises fully in cloth, producing 120 units. Foreign specialises in wheat, producing 240/4 = 60 units. At 1 cloth per wheat, Home obtains each unit of wheat for 1 cloth, which is 1 hour of labour, instead of the 2 hours it would take to grow it. Foreign obtains each unit of cloth for 1 wheat, which is 4 hours, instead of 6 hours making it at home. For example, if Home exports 50 cloth for 50 wheat, it consumes 70 cloth and 50 wheat. In autarky, producing 50 wheat would use 100 hours and leave only 20 cloth. Foreign consumes 10 wheat and 50 cloth, against at most 10 wheat and 33.3 cloth in autarky. Both consume outside their production possibility frontiers, and real wages measured in the imported good rise in both countries.

(d) First, with a single factor every worker gains, so the model cannot explain why trade is politically contentious. Heckscher-Ohlin (through Stolper-Samuelson) and the specific factors model show that some groups lose. Second, it predicts complete specialisation and inter-industry trade, whereas much real trade is intra-industry between similar countries, which is better explained by increasing returns and product differentiation (Krugman) and firm heterogeneity (Melitz). It also ignores trade costs, which gravity models show are central. Its core insight, that comparative rather than absolute advantage drives trade, nonetheless holds up well, and Costinot and Donaldson's work on agriculture finds Ricardian predictions broadly supported.

questions.q:
Lindoria is a small open economy importing steel. Domestic demand is Qd = 200 − 2P and domestic supply is Qs = 3P − 50, where P is the price in £ per tonne. The world price is £40.
(a) Calculate imports under free trade.
(b) Lindoria imposes a tariff of £5 per tonne. Calculate the new price, domestic production, consumption and imports.
(c) Calculate the change in consumer surplus, producer surplus, tariff revenue and net welfare.
(d) Lindoria's steelmakers argue the tariff protects an infant industry. Evaluate this argument.
markScheme: Free trade: Qd = 120, Qs = 70, imports = 50
Tariff: P = 45; Qd = 110, Qs = 85, imports = 25
Revenue = 5 × 25 = 125
DWL split: production 37.5, consumption 25
Infant industry: learning-by-doing, dynamic economies; needs market failure (capital markets, spillovers)
Problems: picking winners, political capture and permanence, subsidy better than tariff (targets production without consumption distortion)
Mill-Bastable test; WTO constraints
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) At P = 40: Qd = 200 − 80 = 120 and Qs = 120 − 50 = 70, so imports are 50 tonnes.

(b) A small country cannot affect the world price, so the domestic price rises by the full tariff to £45. Then Qd = 200 − 90 = 110, Qs = 135 − 50 = 85, and imports fall to 25.

(c) Consumer surplus falls by the area between the two prices to the left of demand: 5 × (120 + 110)/2 = 575. Producer surplus rises by 5 × (70 + 85)/2 = 387.5. Tariff revenue is 5 × 25 = 125. The net welfare change is −575 + 387.5 + 125 = −62.5. This is two deadweight triangles: a production distortion of ½ × 5 × 15 = 37.5, as high-cost domestic output replaces cheaper imports, and a consumption distortion of ½ × 5 × 10 = 25, as buyers forgo units worth more than the world price.

(d) The infant-industry argument, associated with Hamilton and List, claims that new producers face high initial costs that fall with experience (learning by doing). Temporary protection lets them reach world competitiveness, after which the tariff can be removed. For the argument to justify intervention, there must be a market failure. If future profits will cover early losses, private investors should fund them unless capital markets are imperfect, or unless learning spills over to other firms that cannot be charged for it. The Mill-Bastable test requires that the industry eventually becomes competitive and that future gains exceed the present value of the costs, including the £62.5 annual deadweight loss here. In practice, governments struggle to pick winners, protected industries lobby to keep tariffs indefinitely, and a production subsidy would achieve the same output effect without taxing consumers, avoiding the consumption distortion. WTO commitments also limit new tariffs. Steel is a capital-intensive industry with global overcapacity, so Lindoria's case looks weak unless strong spillovers can be shown.

questions.q: "Globalisation has made rich countries as a whole better off, but left large groups of workers worse off. Governments should respond with protection." Critically evaluate this statement.
markScheme: Aggregate gains: comparative advantage, variety and scale (Krugman), productivity reallocation (Melitz), ACR formula
Distributional losses: Stolper-Samuelson, specific factors
Evidence: China shock (Autor, Dorn and Hanson 2013) localised and persistent losses; slow adjustment, low mobility
Political consequences: links to populist voting; Brexit vote linked to import exposure (Colantone and Stanig 2018)
Protection costs: 2018–19 US tariffs passed through to US prices (Amiti, Redding and Weinstein 2019; Fajgelbaum et al. 2020), retaliation hurt farmers
Tariffs on intermediates harm downstream producers in value chains; jobs saved costly
Protection is poorly targeted; compensation principle: winners can compensate losers
Alternatives: trade adjustment assistance (US TAA evidence mixed), place-based policy, retraining, wage insurance, progressive taxation
Legitimate exceptions: national security, supply-chain resilience, strategic sectors
Conclusion: first half largely correct; second half usually wrong; compensation and adjustment better
questions.modelAnswer:
Trade theory predicts aggregate gains. Ricardian specialisation, Krugman's gains from scale and variety, and Melitz's reallocation towards productive firms all raise national income. Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodríguez-Clare (2012) show that these gains can be quantified from domestic expenditure shares and trade elasticities, and estimates for open economies are substantial.

Theory also predicts losers. Under Stolper-Samuelson, rich countries' scarce factor, less-skilled labour, loses as the relative price of labour-intensive goods falls. In the specific-factors model, workers tied to import-competing industries lose. The evidence confirms concentrated harm. Autor, Dorn and Hanson (2013) found that US commuting zones more exposed to Chinese imports suffered persistent manufacturing job losses, lower wages and rising benefit claims, with little migration out. Adjustment was far slower than textbook models assume. Colantone and Stanig (2018) linked regional import exposure to higher Leave voting in the UK's 2016 referendum, which shows the political costs. The first half of the statement is therefore well supported.

The policy conclusion is much weaker. Recent protection has been expensive and poorly targeted. Amiti, Redding and Weinstein (2019) and Fajgelbaum et al. (2020) found that the 2018–19 US tariffs were almost fully passed on to US buyers, and retaliation hit US farmers. Because production runs through global value chains, tariffs on intermediate inputs such as steel raise costs for downstream manufacturers, which employ more workers than the protected sector. Protection also does nothing for workers already displaced.

The compensation principle suggests a better route. Winners gain enough to compensate losers, so the issue is making compensation happen. Options include trade adjustment assistance (US evidence is mixed but positive for training uptake), wage insurance, place-based investment for left-behind regions, and progressive tax and transfer systems.

Some protection is defensible on non-economic grounds: national security, supply-chain resilience in strategic goods such as semiconductors or medicines, and responses to unfair subsidies within WTO rules. These are targeted exceptions, not a general strategy.

The statement's diagnosis is right, but its prescription is mostly wrong. The losses call for credible adjustment and compensation policies rather than tariffs that impose costs widely while helping few.

questions.q:
A regulator wants to cut emissions from two factories by 50 tonnes in total. Factory A has marginal abatement cost MAC_A = 4a_A and Factory B has MAC_B = a_B, where a is tonnes abated.
(a) Find the cost-effective allocation of abatement and the total cost.
(b) Compare this with a uniform standard requiring each factory to abate 25 tonnes.
(c) Show how a tax or a tradable permit scheme could achieve the cost-effective outcome, and state the tax rate or permit price.
(d) Discuss why governments might prefer one instrument over the other in practice.
markScheme: Cost-effectiveness: MAC_A = MAC_B, so 4a_A = a_B, with a_A + a_B = 50
a_A = 10, a_B = 40, common MAC = 40
Tax of £40/tonne: each firm abates until MAC = 40
Permits: issue allowances for the required emissions; trading leads A to buy permits from B; equilibrium price 40
Equivalence with certainty; allocation affects distribution not efficiency

Practical: revenue raising/double dividend versus free allocation for political acceptability; certainty of emissions versus price; Weitzman; price volatility (EU ETS), leakage; hybrid price floors (UK Carbon Price Floor)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Total abatement cost is minimised when marginal costs are equal, otherwise shifting a tonne from the high-cost to the low-cost factory saves money. Setting 4a_A = a_B with a_A + a_B = 50 gives 5a_A = 50, so a_A = 10 and a_B = 40, both at a marginal cost of 40. Total cost is the area under each MAC curve: 2a_A² + ½a_B² = 2(100) + ½(1,600) = 200 + 800 = 1,000.

(b) With 25 tonnes each, costs are 2(625) = 1,250 for A and ½(625) = 312.5 for B, totalling 1,562.5. The uniform standard wastes 562.5, over 50% more, because A's marginal cost (100) far exceeds B's (25) at that allocation.

(c) With a tax of £40 per tonne emitted, each factory abates until its MAC equals 40: A abates 10 and B abates 40. Under a permit scheme, the regulator issues allowances equal to baseline emissions minus 50. However permits are initially allocated, A, with high abatement costs, will buy permits from B until both MACs equal the permit price. Equilibrium is again at 40. With certainty, the two instruments are equivalent in efficiency. The allocation of permits, free or auctioned, affects only who bears the cost.

(d) A tax raises revenue that can cut other distorting taxes, the possible "double dividend", and gives price certainty for investment. A cap guarantees the environmental outcome, which suits legally binding targets such as the UK's carbon budgets. Weitzman (1974) shows that under cost uncertainty a tax is better when marginal damages are flat, as for CO₂ in the short run. Permits can be grandfathered to win industry support, at the cost of windfall profits, as in the early EU ETS. Permit prices can also be volatile: the EU ETS price collapsed after over-allocation until the Market Stability Reserve tightened supply. Many systems therefore use hybrids. The UK's Carbon Price Floor topped up the EU price for power generators, and price floors and ceilings combine price stability with quantity control. Concern about carbon leakage has led to border adjustment mechanisms in the EU and planned in the UK.

questions.q: "Disagreement over the right policy response to climate change is mainly a disagreement about ethics, not economics." Discuss with reference to the Stern-Nordhaus debate and later contributions.
markScheme: Explains social cost of carbon and its role in optimal carbon pricing
Ramsey rule r = ρ + ηg
Stern (2006): ρ = 0.1%, η = 1, giving low discount rates (~1.4%), high SCC, urgent action
Nordhaus DICE: calibrated to market returns, higher r, lower SCC, gradual ramp
Ethical parameters: ρ (intergenerational equity), η (inequality aversion, also across countries); descriptive versus prescriptive approaches (Arrow et al.)
Empirical/scientific uncertainties: climate sensitivity, damage functions, tipping points
Weitzman (2009) fat tails: catastrophic risk dominates, making discounting less decisive
Declining discount rates for long horizons (UK Green Book; Weitzman 1998 gamma discounting)
Political economy and policy design disagreements: instruments, leakage, international free-riding (Nordhaus climate clubs 2015), technology
Later convergence: updated DICE versions and US SCC estimates rising; agreement on carbon pricing
Conclusion: ethics central to the level of SCC but not the only disagreement
questions.modelAnswer:
The social cost of carbon (SCC) is the present value of future damages from an extra tonne of CO₂, and in a first-best world it sets the carbon price. The Ramsey rule r = ρ + ηg breaks this down into pure time preference ρ, the elasticity of marginal utility η and consumption growth g.

The Stern Review (2006) set ρ = 0.1%, reflecting only a small extinction risk, on the ethical ground that future generations' welfare counts equally. With η = 1 and growth of about 1.3%, the discount rate is about 1.4%. This implies a high SCC and early abatement. Nordhaus, using his DICE model, calibrated parameters so that the implied discount rate matched observed market returns of about 4–5%. This gave a much lower SCC and an optimal "policy ramp" with gradually rising carbon prices. Nordhaus himself showed that running DICE with Stern's ρ and η produced Stern-like urgency. This is the choice between a prescriptive approach (ethics sets ρ and η) and a descriptive one (markets reveal them). The parameter η is also ethical, since it measures aversion to inequality between generations and between rich and poor countries.

The disagreement is not only ethical. The SCC depends on equilibrium climate sensitivity, damage functions and the possibility of tipping points, all of which are deeply uncertain. Weitzman (2009) argued that fat-tailed catastrophe risk can dominate cost-benefit analysis, making the discount-rate debate less decisive than the treatment of extreme outcomes. Uncertainty about future growth also supports declining long-horizon discount rates (Weitzman, 1998), as adopted in the UK Green Book. Updated damage estimates have pushed published SCC values well above early figures.

Policy disagreement also extends beyond the SCC. Instrument choice, carbon leakage, innovation policy and international free-riding all matter. Nordhaus (2015) proposed climate clubs with trade penalties for non-members.

Ethics drives much of the disagreement over how fast to cut emissions, but scientific uncertainty, the treatment of catastrophic risk and policy design are also central. Economists broadly agree that carbon should be priced; the debate is over how high and how.
